newsitem.title: UK: HK's Patten shrugs off Chinese insults.
newsitem.headline: HK's Patten shrugs off Chinese insults.

text.p: Chris Patten, Britain's last governor of Hong Kong before it is handed back to Beijing, on Tuesday shrugged off Chinese insults and said he preferred them to malicious British jibes.
Patten has been reviled as "a serpent" and "a villain for 1,000 antiquities" for championing civil rights in the runup to the handover that marks the end of 156 years of British rule.
Patten, interviewed by Harpers and Queen magazine at his Hong Kong residence, said he never lost a wink of sleep over the insults.
"I'll tell you this: it's always more tiresome to hear the cutlery behind your shoulders. There's a particular English style about being malicious which is rather unattractive" he told the magazine.
Patten, who masterminded Prime Minister John Major's shock 1992 election victory but lost his own seat in parliament, confessed he could not understand Chinese fears of losing face.
"The whole concept of face is a puzzle. I recognise it exists, but I'm slightly alarmed when people think it might affect me as well," he said.

Patten, who has ruled out challenging for the Conservative leadership now Major is to step down after his crushing election defeat, plans to start writing when he leaves Hong Kong for his house in France.
"It will not be a political memoir about Hong Kong -- that would be pretty boring," he said.

"What I want to write about are some of the issues which have been raised by the time I've spent here: how curious it is that we should have this responsibility at the end of the 20th century, whether there are such things as Asian values, the relationship between economic growth and the rule of law."
